messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Emmett Hernandez sat at his pottery wheel, hands hesitating over the lump of clay in front of him. It had been months since he'd last created anything worthwhile, and even longer since his wife, Maria, had passed away. He couldn't shake the feeling that every time he tried to get back into his craft, he was somehow betraying her memory. The smell of damp earth and clay usually brought him comfort, but now it only served as a harsh reminder of all the things they used to do together. As he struggled to focus on the task at hand, Emmett's mind began to wander back to the day Maria died. He remembered the hospital room, the beeping machines, and the numbness that had washed over him when the doctor delivered the news. It was as if time had stood still in that moment, and everything since then had been a blur. The grief felt like a weight he couldn't shake, always lurking just beneath the surface. Emmett found himself pushing away any positive emotions that dared to creep in. When friends or family tried to console him with stories of Maria's warmth and kindness, he'd change the subject or politely excuse himself. It wasn't that he didn't appreciate their efforts; it was just that allowing himself to feel good – even for a moment – felt like he was somehow diminishing his love for her. Avoiding anything that reminded him of Maria had become second nature. Emmett would take detours on his daily walks to avoid passing by the park where they used to picnic, and he'd stopped attending pottery classes because the instructor's voice sounded too much like Maria's. Even small things, like cooking his favorite meals or listening to their shared playlist, felt like a betrayal. Making plans for the future had also become impossible. Emmett would get anxious at the mere suggestion of booking a vacation or planning a project beyond the next few days. What was the point, anyway? Without Maria by his side, everything felt uncertain and scary. His friends and family tried to reassure him that life went on, but Emmett couldn't shake the feeling that he was just going through the motions. As the weeks turned into months, Emmett's avoidance behaviors had started to take a toll on his relationships. His children were worried about him, his friends felt like they'd lost touch, and even his pottery wheel gathered dust in the corner of the room. It was as if Emmett had built a wall around himself, and he didn't know how to tear it down. One day, as he sat amidst the silence of his studio, Emmett realized that he couldn't keep living like this. The pain wasn't going away, but maybe – just maybe – it was time to start facing it head-on. With a newfound sense of determination, he slowly began to clean up his workspace and prepare for a new project. It wouldn't be easy, but for the first time in months, Emmett felt like he might finally be ready to take the next step forward.
